title: Recursive Operator Localization and Spectral Gap Descent via the Geometry of Local Spectral Expansion
abstract: We introduce Recursive Operator Localization (ROL), a framework for constructing hierarchies of local energy problems linked by linear maps between Hilbert spaces. To address spectral-gap problems, including those arising in quantum systems, we study a realization of ROL by nested subspaces indexed by a weighted simplicial complex. Using spectral gaps of auxiliary classical random walks on links, we propagate geometric estimates upward and use them to turn local spectral gaps at the bottom of the hierarchy into a spectral-gap bound for the global operator. For weighted scalar-valued functions on facets, the ROL decomposition becomes the law of total variance, recovering classical spectral-gap bounds from local link expansion (Alev and Lau, STOC 2020). Moreover, for positive binary spin distributions, conditional influence describes the overlap of the corresponding subspaces, yielding known heat-bath gap bounds from spectral independence (Anari, Liu, and Oveis Gharan, FOCS 2020). The framework also offers a route toward quantum Gibbs sampling, with applications requiring model-specific geometric estimates and energy comparisons.
summary: This paper introduces Recursive Operator Localization (ROL), a powerful mathematical framework designed to compute global spectral gaps by analyzing local energy problems hierarchically. It achieves this by quantifying the 'gluing defect'—the energy cost required to reconcile local minimum choices—and incorporating this into a recursive bound. This methodology provides a general tool for analyzing the mixing times and spectral properties of complex quantum and classical systems.
main_problem: The paper develops a general framework to derive global spectral-gap bounds for complex operators by recursively combining local spectral estimates.
main_result: It establishes that the global spectral gap can be bounded by a combination of local energy bounds, norm-retention factors, and the accumulated 'gluing defect' costs across a hierarchical decomposition structure.
method: The core method is Recursive Operator Localization (ROL), which constructs energy hierarchies linked by linear maps between Hilbert spaces, allowing local estimates to propagate globally.
model_or_system: The framework is abstract, applying to operators on Hilbert spaces derived from local energy problems, with realizations including quantum Markov semigroups and weighted functions on simplicial complexes.
key_observables: Spectral Gap, Effective Energy ($E_{	ext{eff}}$), Gluing Defect ($\Delta_	au(b)$), Norm-Retention Factor ($	heta_	au$).
important_parameters: The structure depends on the choice of localization maps, energy definitions, and the geometry of the underlying complex.
main_assumptions: The descent argument relies on discarding the non-negative defect term in the main gap bound, and the full recursive application requires careful tracking of subspaces.

paper_structure: The paper introduces ROL, details the recursive decomposition theorem relating global energy to local energies and defects, provides specific mathematical propositions (like Proposition 7.1) for bounding the defect, and discusses applications to classical and quantum sampling.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical machinery connecting local spectral information (like those found in local Hamiltonians or small subsystems) to global spectral properties is highly valuable for analyzing complex, large-scale quantum systems where direct computation is intractable.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Retained spaces along a localization path. Left: along one selected path ∅→τ →ν in the hierarchy, retained data are successively localized in the spaces I∅, Iτ, and Iν. The nested regions illustrate the intuition of a subspace realization; general ROL spaces need not be subspaces of a common ambient space, nor is strict dimension decrease required at every step. Right: the same path is highlighted within a branching hierarchy. In a hierarchy indexed by faces of a simplicial complex, a child has the form ν = τi := τ ∪{i}, where i is a vertex of the link of τ.

Figure 2: An overview of descent. Left: for one parent–child pair, Eτ,ib is the component removed by localization, lying in Uτ,i ⊆Iτ. Right: geometry across branches and spectral expansion of the classical link walks (illustrated in Figure 8) control average norm loss through the hierarchy. This allows local energy bounds to be transported upward to a global spectral gap under the descent assumptions.

Figure 3: Ordered paths in a simplicial-link hierarchy. For the full tetrahedron X (including its interior), taking the link at i and then at j, or at j and then at i, gives the same full edge on {k, ℓ}. Taking its link at k leaves the vertex ℓ. Each triangle is filled. The two colored routes select the orders (i, j, k) and (j, i, k). This diagram describes link operations, not elimination of operator variables.

Figure 4: Root paths and their prefixes in a chosen localization hierarchy. On the left, paths p and q merge at the same index ij and have the same endpoint t(p) = t(q) = ijk. On the right, each tree vertex represents an entire prefix, labelled only by its endpoint for brevity. The internal prefixes are the empty path, (∅→i), (∅→j), (∅→i →ij), and (∅→j →ij). A prefix shared by several stopped paths is counted once, but different prefixes with the same endpoint remain distinct. Paths s, t stop at depth two, whereas p, q stop at depth three.

Figure 5: One-step localization and depth-two decomposition (Lemma 3.7 and Corollary 3.8). Each node carries an effective problem. Teal nodes are the endpoints where the displayed decomposition stops. Panel (a) assembles all outgoing steps at any depth. Panel (b) applies this operation at the root and at every depth-one node. Two outgoing steps are shown only for illustration. The tree layout separates paths for readability; their endpoints need not be distinct nodes of the underlying hierarchy.
